header.tag_why: The deal turned when Wen priced the manual matching from the controller's own statements and Ines accepted it as 'that's my number, not yours'; the reconciliation capability got her attention, but the money case on her own data is what closed it.

evidence.excerpt: I thought it was the online ordering portal. That's what the inbound said.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: they had a new CFO. Ines. She'd been there about four months, and her first month-end close took nine days.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: two people in finance matching deposits from the bank against the processor statements against invoices in the ERP. By hand, in spreadsheets.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I didn't get this until maybe the third call
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: The inbound named an IT project, but the money and the urgency came from a new CFO whose first close took nine days. The portal was off the shelf with a plugin, so there was little for us to win on checkout anyway. We ran about three calls and one proposal against the visible project before anyone asked what finance was suffering from.
trigger.messaging: When an inbound names a commerce project at a non-tech business, discovery and the first deck should ask how long month-end close takes and who matches deposits, and lead with M9 when the answer hurts.

evidence.excerpt: I can recommend, she decides.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: And she's the one who signed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Paul had forwarded it to her, she read the first page and said it wasn't her problem.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Paul was polite about it. Ines wasn't on that call, thank god.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Paul relayed the decision rather than making it. Our APIs-and-checkout proposal reached the real decider only by forwarding, and she judged it on page one. Paul's politeness on the first call hid that the decision sat elsewhere, and that cost three weeks of silence.
decider.messaging: The first page of any proposal that may be forwarded to finance has to state the close-time and reconciliation problem in CFO terms before any API or checkout content.

evidence.excerpt: I honestly don't know what Fiserv showed them, if anything. I never saw a deck.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: we can take a look at your rates.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I didn't ask about my rates.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: She did ask us one new thing afterwards, whether she'd get a named contact.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: The incumbent bank treated her outreach as a price question. She rejected that framing, so rate was not the contest, and no other competitor appears in the transcript. The only change in her questions after the bank call was asking for a named contact, prompted by her bank rep changing without her knowing who replaced them. Our M5 message (tiered response times) answers a different question than the one she asked, which was who her person is. What Fiserv actually pitched is unknown.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-bundled incumbents, don't lead on rates; position visibility into deposits plus a named contact, and reword M5 around a named person rather than response tiers.

evidence.excerpt: Silence was the whole opening. I ran the standard first-call deck.

evidence.excerpt: Paul's team is four people and they aren't building anything. The portal is off the shelf with a plugin.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: The reaction was the payout reconciliation.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: go back.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: M1 (global, every currency) and M2 (developers) both missed a three-state seller with a four-person IT team that isn't building anything. The one thing that landed, payout reconciliation (M9), sits deep in our list. The decider herself stopped the demo to see it again and then asked to see it on her own data. Our standard opener nearly lost the deal.
message.messaging: For regional, finance-led buyers, open with M9 framed as faster month-end close and hold M1 and M2 back unless the prospect is global or builds its own software.

decided.insight: The deal moved from what the rep called dead to signed on one artifact: a cost of manual matching built from one month of the customer's statements, with the controller in the room. Ines's line rejects exactly what M6 offers, which is someone else's study. The proof that worked was hers. The exact dollar figure is not known; the rep recalls only low six figures a year.
decided.messaging: Rewrite M6 from 'independent economic impact study' to an offer: send one month of statements and we'll show what manual reconciliation costs you, in your numbers.

gaps.insight: M8 has no proof for invoice-driven wholesale businesses. Sending a retail story signaled that we didn't understand her business, and she raised the missing reference twice. Her question about 14 branches' counter readers landing in the same report was answered with a slide, never shown. The transcript does not establish whether the branches actually moved to us, so the unified claim (M3) is untested here.
gaps.messaging: Build a distributor/wholesale customer story with a reference willing to take calls, and add a demo of counter-terminal sales landing in the same reconciliation report as online sales.

language.messaging: Test a finance-buyer line built on her words, along the lines of: know where your money is, with every deposit matched to its invoices before month-end, instead of 'financial infrastructure'.

close.rep_takeaway: When the inbound names a project, ask early who feels the pain behind it and who signs. Then ask for the customer's own data: one month of statements turned a deal you had at 20 percent into 'that's my number, not yours.'
